text: Every parameter you've passed so far has been one value at a time. But what if you need to hand a stored procedure fifty new order lines in a single call, instead of calling it fifty times or packing everything into one giant delimited string? That's what a table-valued parameter is for.

First you need a type. Create type dbo dot OrderLineItemList as table, with ProductID, OrderQty, UnitPrice. It looks like a table definition because it is one — just a reusable shape you can now use as a parameter type.

Then a procedure parameter declared with that type — at Items, dbo dot OrderLineItemList, READONLY. That keyword is required: a table-valued parameter can be read from inside the procedure, joined, filtered, selected — but never inserted into, updated, or deleted from.

To call it, declare a variable of that same table type, insert a few rows into it, then pass the variable in as the argument. Every row travels to the server in one call — one round trip, one execution, no loop and nothing to parse.

Before table-valued parameters existed, this meant one of two things: calling the procedure once per row — slow, a round trip for every single row — or packing everything into a comma or XML delimited string and parsing it apart inside the procedure, which gets fragile fast with embedded delimiters or special characters. A TVP replaces both with a real, typed table.

That closes out Chapter 7's programming topics — variables, branching, loops, cursors, stored procedures, dynamic SQL, MERGE, functions, triggers, and now table-valued parameters. Chapter 8 moves into transactions — making sure a whole sequence of statements either all succeed together, or none of them do.
